Pass passwords through variables whose name contains `PASSWORD` (or `TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `KEY`): **Starter stack…** masks those.

The **New sandbox** dialog shows the chosen template's `compose.yaml`; edit it there, or pick `empty` and paste your own (`empty` without a compose text is refused). The sandbox then gets that text (comments kept, the same variables filled in, the template's `before_script` still run) and shows "(edited)" in the list and its panel. The text is checked first: it must be YAML with at least one service, at most 256 KB, that docker compose accepts. Keys that would make the compose CLI (which runs in the Purgatorium container) read the server's files are refused: `build`, `env_file`, `label_file`, `extends.file`, `include`, and `secrets`/`configs` from a `file` or `environment` — build images through `DOCKER_HOST` or Portainer instead. The CLI gets no Purgatorium settings in its environment, so an unknown `${VAR}` is empty.

# Sleep and wake

A sandbox is **running**, **asleep** (containers stopped, data intact), in **deep sleep** (containers and network removed, data intact) or **archived** (after an explicit delete). There is no fixed-time expiry: a sandbox only sleeps when nobody uses it, and only a person deleting it removes it.

Handled entirely by [Sablier](https://github.com/sablierapp/sablier). The sandbox's outer containers (DinD, frps, socat) form one Sablier group and its Traefik router carries the Sablier middleware. After `idle_timeout` without HTTP traffic the group is stopped — which stops everything inside the sandbox too. The sandbox's router exists only while it runs, so the next request reaches Purgatorium's catch-all `/wake`, which wakes it within the owner's limits (see [Web UI and sign-in](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/web-ui/index.md)) and shows a waiting page until the router is back; the socat healthcheck only passes once the FRP tunnel is online (an app's HTTP proxy, or for a stack that publishes no port, frpc's readiness marker for 15 seconds). Sablier still measures the idle time and puts the sandbox to sleep. **Reset** next to *Sleeps in* in the panel (`POST /sandboxes/:name/keep-awake`) starts the countdown over, as a visit would; it does not wake a sleeping sandbox.

> **Apps must set a restart policy to come back after sleep.** When the sandbox wakes, its inner Docker daemon only restarts containers with `restart: unless-stopped` or `restart: always`. Without one, the app stays stopped and has to be started by hand (`docker start`, or from Portainer):
>
> ```
> services:
>   web:
>     image: my-app
>     restart: unless-stopped
>   db:
>     image: postgres:16
>     restart: unless-stopped
> ```

HTTP traffic through Traefik counts as activity, and so does traffic on a Docker connection (`DOCKER_HOST=tcp://<raw>-docker.<domain>:443`): Purgatorium renews the session once a minute while bytes go through it. A Docker connection that is only open does not count, and a Docker connection never wakes a sleeping sandbox: Docker Desktop keeps every context connected for its Builds view and reconnects at once, so it would wake the sandbox each time it fell asleep. Wake it first (**Wake**, `POST /sandboxes/:name/start`, or open one of its apps); until then `docker` cannot connect. Sablier persists its sessions (`--storage.file`), so restarting Sablier does not put running sandboxes to sleep. A sandbox started without Purgatorium (Docker restarting it, `docker compose start` by hand, or Purgatorium restarted while it was starting one) has no session at first; Purgatorium notices within two minutes and opens one, so it still sleeps after its `idle_timeout`. After a host reboot, sandboxes that were asleep stay asleep.

The sandbox list (`GET /sandboxes` adds `stops_at`, `deep_sleep_at` and `deep_sleep_after` to each row) and the details panel show **Sleeps in** (time until Sablier stops a running sandbox; every request resets it — read from Sablier's `/metrics`, which Purgatorium reaches on `sablier-net`) and **Deep sleep in** (time until an asleep sandbox is taken down).

Both times can be changed after creation — **Change…** next to *Sleep* on the panel's **Details** tab, or `PATCH /sandboxes/<name>` with `{"idle_timeout": "45m", "deep_sleep_after": "14d"}` (either field; same formats as at creation; owner or admin). The values are written into the sandbox's `docker-compose.yml`. A new `idle_timeout` recreates only the socat container, which carries the Sablier middleware labels: a running sandbox's apps are unreachable for a few seconds, an asleep one stays asleep, and the DinD container and its inner stack are not touched; it applies from the next request's Sablier session. A new `deep_sleep_after` applies immediately — Purgatorium reads it from the compose file.

`idle_timeout` takes seconds, minutes, hours or days (`30s`, `30m`, `2h`, `1d`); days are kept as hours (`1d` becomes `24h`), because Sablier's durations have no days. `deep_sleep_after` takes `m`, `h` or `d`. The server can set a ceiling for users' sandboxes: `SANDBOX_MAX_IDLE_TIMEOUT` and `SANDBOX_MAX_DEEP_SLEEP_AFTER` ([Configuration](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/configuration/index.md)); a value above it, or never, is refused (*at most 2h on this server*). `0` or `off` means never, for both — at creation and when changing them. `deep_sleep_after: off` never takes the sandbox down. Sablier has no "never", so `idle_timeout: off` is written as a 10-year session (`87600h`): the sandbox keeps running, and if it is stopped by hand the next request still wakes it. The panel and the list show "never" for either.

# CPU, memory and disk

## CPU and memory

Every sandbox runs with a CPU and memory limit: the sandbox and everything inside it share it (the inner containers live in the sandbox container's cgroup). New sandboxes get `SANDBOX_CPUS` / `SANDBOX_MEMORY` (default 2 CPUs, 4 GB); on create (**Advanced**) or later (**Resources…** in the panel, `PATCH /sandboxes/:name` with `cpus`, `memory`) a user can raise their sandbox's limits up to `SANDBOX_MAX_CPUS` / `SANDBOX_MAX_MEMORY` (default 4 and 8 GB), the admin up to the host's size. A change applies at once without a restart (`docker update`) and is kept in the sandbox's compose file. Memory below what a running sandbox uses now is refused (stop it first). There is no swap beyond the memory limit.

The panel shows the sandbox's current CPU and memory against its limits (sampled every 10 s), and the list a short *CPU · Mem* column for running sandboxes. The API gives `limits` (`cpus`, `memory` in bytes) and, for a running sandbox, `usage` (`cpu` in cores, `memory`, `memory_limit`).

## Disk

Everything a sandbox keeps (its inner images, containers and volumes) is in its own `docker_data` volume. Purgatorium measures it from outside with `du`: a running sandbox every 15 minutes, an asleep one once after it stopped (its size does not change while it sleeps); the results are kept in `data/disk-usage.json`. The **Resources** tab shows the use against the sandbox's disk limit, `SANDBOX_DISK` (20 GB by default); the admin can set another one per sandbox (**Change limits…**, or `PATCH /sandboxes/:name` with `disk`).

Above the limit the panel and the sandbox list show ⚠ and suggest cleaning up (`docker system prune` in the sandbox). It is **only a warning**: nothing is stopped or refused, and a sandbox can use more until the host's disk is full. A hard limit (a fixed-size disk per sandbox) is on the [roadmap](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/roadmap/index.md).

# Deep sleep

A sandbox that has been asleep for `deep_sleep_after` (template field, default `7d`, `off` disables; overridable per sandbox on create) is taken down with `compose down`: its containers and its network are removed, its volumes and `opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/` stay. The volumes hold everything a user keeps: the sandbox's inner Docker (`docker_data`: images, inner containers and their volumes) and the sandbox's own `/opt`, `/root`, `/home` and `/srv`, so nothing written there is lost when the container is recreated (deep sleep, or a container removed by hand). Anything else in the sandbox container's file system (e.g. packages installed with `apk add`) is not kept. This frees Docker networks, which are limited. Purgatorium checks every `DEEP_SLEEP_CHECK_INTERVAL` (default `1m`).

The panel's **Details** tab says when a sandbox that is asleep or in deep sleep last ran (*Last ran: 3 weeks ago*; `last_running_at` in `GET /sandboxes/:name`), and so do its apps on the [Hub](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/hub/index.md). Purgatorium keeps that time when it takes the sandbox down; for one taken down before it did, the time is an estimate, marked `~`.

Requests for a deep-sleeping sandbox have no sandbox router, so they reach Purgatorium's catch-all `/wake`, which rebuilds the stack (`compose up`) and shows a waiting page that updates until the app answers — usually 20–60 s. From then on Sablier handles it as usual. The API reports such sandboxes with `status: "deep_sleep"`, and `POST /sandboxes/:name/start` (**Wake** in the UI) brings them up. **Deep sleep now** on the panel's **Details** tab (`POST /sandboxes/:name/deep-sleep`) takes a sandbox down right away, without waiting for `deep_sleep_after`.

An asleep sandbox whose containers point at a network that no longer exists is taken down the same way at the next check, whatever its `deep_sleep_after`. This happens after `docker compose down` on the Purgatorium stack, which removes and re-creates `traefik-net`: without it, Sablier could never start the sandbox again (exit code 128, "network … not found") and its waiting page would spin forever. The next request rebuilds it on the current networks; its data volume is kept.

# Delete = archive

`DELETE /sandboxes/:name` never discards data. It:

1. stops the sandbox;
1. writes every Docker volume of the sandbox's compose project to `opt/archive/<owner>/<name>-<timestamp>/volumes/<volume>.tar.gz` (the DinD data volume holds all inner images, containers and volumes);
1. copies `opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/` (compose files, certs, credentials) to `.../config/` and writes `manifest.json` (with the owner);
1. only then removes the containers, the volumes and `opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/` (and the owner's directory once it is empty). If any archive step fails nothing is removed and the call returns 500.

Afterwards the name is free again and the sandbox URL returns 404. Archives are never pruned automatically; expect a few hundred MB per sandbox, more with large images.

Restoring by hand:

```
A=opt/archive/alice@example.com/p9m-alice-2026-09-26T21-47-01-401Z
mkdir -p opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com
cp -r $A/config opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com/p9m-alice
for f in $A/volumes/*.tar.gz; do
  v=$(basename $f .tar.gz)
  docker volume create --label com.docker.compose.project=p9m-alice $v
  docker run --rm -v $v:/data -v "$PWD/$A/volumes":/archive alpine tar xzf /archive/$v.tar.gz -C /data
done
docker compose -f opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com/p9m-alice/docker-compose.yml up -d
```

# Isolation and TCP addresses

## Isolation between sandboxes

An app in one sandbox must not reach another sandbox's apps. Today:

- inner containers' private addresses are only reachable inside their own sandbox;
- Sablier's API is on its own network (`sablier-net`) shared only with Traefik;
- a port an inner container *publishes* on all interfaces (`9000:9000`) gets a link (its tunnel) and a TLS TCP address, and other sandboxes can also reach it directly on its `traefik-net` address; a port published on `127.0.0.1` (`127.0.0.1:9000:9000`) is private to the sandbox: no link, no TCP address, no neighbour. A link whose app does not answer is marked ⚠ in the panel — usually the app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside its container; make it listen on 0.0.0.0.

The Purgatorium API itself requires authentication (see [Web UI and sign-in](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/web-ui/index.md)). Two endpoints of each sandbox are not published on the host but are reachable from other sandboxes over `traefik-net`: its Docker API (protected by per-sandbox TLS client certs) and its frps API (`:7500`, which lists the sandbox's proxies; it has a per-sandbox password, kept in the sandbox's `frps.toml`, so a neighbour gets 401). Closing published ports to neighbours is on the [roadmap](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/roadmap/index.md).

Who may open an app's **web address** can be limited per app with `p9m.access` ([App access](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/app-access/index.md)); that applies to HTTP through Purgatorium only, not to the TCP addresses below, nor to the direct `traefik-net` path from other sandboxes.

## App web addresses

Each TCP port an inner container publishes on all interfaces gets a web address, `<sandbox>-<project>-<container>-port<host port>.<domain>` (`shop-inner-web-port8080.<domain>`). A label on the container gives it a short one instead:

| Label                                                      | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `p9m.subdomain: web`                                       | The app's address becomes `<sandbox>-web.<domain>`. No other label does (`p7y.subdomain` and `frpc.subdomain` are ignored). `shell` gets no TCP address: that name is the sandbox's own SSH ([Shell and logs](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/shell-and-logs/index.md)). |
| `p9m.access`                                               | Who may open the address ([App access](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/app-access/index.md)).                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `p9m.connect.user`                                         | The login the **Connect…** recipes use (below).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `p9m.publish`, `p9m.title`, `p9m.description`, `p9m.image` | Lists the app on the [Hub](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/hub/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                |

```
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    labels:
      p9m.subdomain: web
```

A container with `p9m.subdomain` that publishes several ports has one web address for all of them; each port's TCP address (below) gets `-port<N>` too.

## TLS TCP addresses

A port an inner container publishes on all interfaces (`"5432:5432"`) also gets a TCP address, its HTTP name plus `-tcp`, on port 443, TLS only: `shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain>:443`. Ports published on `127.0.0.1` stay private: no TCP address and no link.

- Postgres: `psql "host=shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require …"`
- Any client that speaks TLS (Redis `--tls`, MQTTS): connect with that name as SNI.
- SSH through TLS: `ProxyCommand openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h`.

Traefik passes these names through to Purgatorium's TCP gateway, which terminates TLS (with `certs/tls.crt`, or a self-signed `*.<domain>` kept in `data/`), wakes the sandbox if needed and connects to the sandbox container over `traefik-net`. There is no extra authentication: the service's own login protects it. Only web traffic keeps a sandbox awake: without it the sandbox sleeps after its idle timeout even with an open TCP connection, which then drops; the next connection wakes it. Right after a wake the service itself may still be starting (Postgres answers `the database system is starting up`), so let the client retry. The details panel lists the addresses with ready-made commands (**Connect…**), picked by the container's own port (5432 Postgres, 6379 Redis, 22 or 2222 SSH; anything else gets the generic TLS recipe). A `p9m.connect.user` label on the container puts its login into those commands. The API gives the same as `tcp_addresses` (`address`, `port`, `user`) next to `tcp_urls`.

The `tcp-demo` template (on either runtime) shows it end to end. Its starter stack has a Postgres with a sample `orders` table (`<name>-db-tcp`), a Redis (`<name>-redis-tcp`), an SSH server with the user `demo` (`<name>-ssh-tcp`) and pgweb in the browser (`https://<name>-pgweb.<domain>`, user `demo`), all behind one generated password (**Demo password** in the details panel and in **Connect…**). Insert a row with psql and it shows up in pgweb:

```
psql "host=<name>-db-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require user=postgres dbname=postgres" -c "insert into orders (customer, item, amount) values ('me', 'espresso', 3)"
redis-cli -h <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -p 443 --tls --sni <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -a <password> ping   # add --insecure with the self-signed certificate
ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" demo@<name>-ssh-tcp.<domain>
```

The three TCP containers also get an HTTP link in **Apps** (frpc tunnels every published port); those links do not lead anywhere useful.

# SSH, terminal and logs

## SSH into a sandbox

Every sandbox runs an sshd: root, keys only, at `<name>-shell-tcp.<domain>:443` (the same TLS gateway as the TCP addresses). Add your public keys under **My area → SSH keys** (`/settings/ssh-keys`, API `GET/POST/DELETE /ssh-keys`): they let you into all your sandboxes, and a change takes effect at once. A create request can add keys for that sandbox only (`ssh_keys`, or **Advanced → Extra SSH public keys**). Inside, `docker` talks to the sandbox's own Docker.

```
ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" root@<name>-shell-tcp.<domain>
```

Each new sandbox also has a key of its own: **Download key** in its panel (API `GET /sandboxes/:name/ssh-key`; `POST` makes one for an SSH sandbox that has none yet), so nobody has to make or upload a key first. The **Connect…** recipe then reads `ssh -i ~/Downloads/<name>.key …`.

The name `shell` is reserved: an inner service with `p9m.subdomain: shell` gets no TCP address.

## Terminal in the browser

**Terminal** in a sandbox's panel opens a root shell in the sandbox in a new tab: nothing to install, no key. It wakes the sandbox if it is asleep, and keeps it awake while the tab is open. Inside, `docker` talks to the sandbox's own Docker. Only the sandbox's owner (and the admin) can open it, from the Purgatorium pages themselves (signed in; not with a token); at most 5 at once per user.

## Terminal in a container

The **Containers** tab of a sandbox's panel (not in Simple) lists the containers in the sandbox's own Docker: name, compose project and service, image, state (API `GET /sandboxes/:name/containers`). **Terminal** next to a running one opens the same browser terminal, in that container: as the container's own user (its `user:`), in its working directory, with that user's login shell (else bash, else sh). That is the way into an app that only has a console, e.g. Claude Code in a devcontainer. The rules are the terminal's above; closing the tab ends the shell and what runs in it (Claude Code keeps its conversations: `claude --continue` picks up again; or run it in `tmux`).

## App logs

**Logs** in a sandbox's panel opens, in a new tab, what the apps in the sandbox write: the last 100 lines of every container (time, service name; errors in red), then new lines as they come. A filter shows one service; Pause holds new lines, Clear empties the view. It does not wake the sandbox or keep it awake: a sleeping one says *asleep* with a **Start** button. With a token: `curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://p9m.example.com/sandboxes/p9m-shop/logs/stream`. At most 5 viewers per sandbox at once.

# Files

The **Files** tab of a sandbox's panel shows its files: open folders, upload files (**Upload…**, or drop them on the list, several at once) or whole folders with everything in them (**Upload folder…**, or drop the folder; folders on the way that are not there yet are made, empty ones too when dropped), download a file, or a whole folder as a `.tar` (**Download folder**), make folders and delete.

It shows four folders, the ones that are kept when the sandbox goes into deep sleep or its container is recreated: `/root` (where it opens), `/home`, `/srv` and `/opt`. Anything else in the sandbox container is gone then, so it is not offered here.

## The apps' volumes

**Volumes**, next to the four folders, lists the volumes of the apps in the sandbox's own Docker (a database's data, an app's uploads), with their compose project and the containers that use them; open one to browse, upload and download as above. Their files are in the sandbox container already (the sandbox's Docker keeps them under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume>/_data`, in the `docker_data` volume), so nothing extra is started, and they are kept over a deep sleep too. Only the local driver's volumes are shown; a container's own files outside its volumes are not (use `docker cp` in the sandbox for those).

- **A running app:** while a container that uses the volume runs, the tab says so. A copy of a database's files taken while it runs may not be consistent, and the app may not expect files changed under it: stop it first (`docker compose stop db` in the sandbox), or use the database's own dump.
- **Owners:** uploaded files and new folders belong to root, readable by everyone (`0644`). An app running as another user that has to write them needs a `chown` in the sandbox.
- A volume's own folder cannot be deleted here: remove the volume with `docker volume rm`.

The sandbox has to be running: asleep, the tab offers to wake it. A file can be up to `FILES_MAX_UPLOAD` (100 MB by default, see [Configuration](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/configuration/index.md)).

## API and MCP

| Method   | Path                                    |                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files?path=/root/app` | The folder's entries (folders first): `name`, `type` (`dir`, `file`, `link`, `other`), `size`, `mtime`                                                                  |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/content?path=…` | A file's bytes, or a folder as a tar                                                                                                                                    |
| `PUT`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/content?path=…` | Upload: the body is the file (`curl -T report.pdf`); missing folders on the path are made                                                                               |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/text?path=…`    | A text file as `{ path, text }` (UTF-8, up to 1 MB)                                                                                                                     |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/files/mkdir`          | `{"path": "/srv/data"}`                                                                                                                                                 |
| `DELETE` | `/sandboxes/:name/files?path=…`         | A file, or a folder with everything in it                                                                                                                               |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/volumes`              | The apps' volumes: `name`, `path` (e.g. `/var/lib/docker/volumes/shop_db/_data`, for the routes above), `project`, `containers` (`name`, `service`, `running`, `mount`) |

```
curl -T notes.md -H "Authorization: Bearer $P9M_TOKEN" "https://p9m.example.com/sandboxes/p9m-shop/files/content?path=/root/notes.md"
```

A token limited to the sandbox may use all of them. Over [MCP](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/mcp/index.md) they are `list_sandbox_files`, `read_sandbox_file`, `write_sandbox_file` (text), `create_sandbox_folder`, `delete_sandbox_file` and `list_sandbox_volumes`; a download is left out, since a tool result carries no file.

# Hub

The **Hub** lists the apps your team has built, in one place, for the people who *use* them: colleagues who never run a sandbox find an app and open it with one click. It is a web app of its own, at its own address (by default `hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>`), served by Purgatorium but apart from its UI: no sandboxes, no *New sandbox*, no quota.

An app appears on the Hub when a label on its container says so; it shows its title, description, owner and whether it runs or sleeps, and **Open** opens it in a new tab. An app that is asleep wakes on that click, as any request wakes it.

## Turn it on

```
# .env
HUB_ENABLED=true
# HUB_HOST=hub.example.com     # default: hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>
# HUB_TITLE=Example Ltd        # shown in its header
```

then `docker compose up -d`. HTTPS uses the same wildcard certificate as everything else under the domain.

**Single sign-on:** add `https://hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>/auth/callback` at your provider as a second allowed redirect URI (next to Purgatorium's `https://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN>/auth/callback`). The administrator can also sign in to the Hub with the password, so it can be tried without single sign-on.

## Who sees it

| Who      | Settings                                      | May                                                         |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Builders | `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`, `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` | use Purgatorium, create sandboxes, publish, and use the Hub |
| Viewers  | `HUB_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`, `HUB_ALLOWED_EMAILS`   | sign in to the Hub only                                     |

- With `HUB_ALLOWED_*` empty, only builders (and the administrator) use the Hub.
- A viewer who tries Purgatorium's own sign-in is refused with *"You have access to the Hub only: https://hub.example.com"*, and gets no Purgatorium session or token.
- Taken off a list: signed out of the Hub at the next request.

## Publish an app

Add labels to its container in the stack you deploy into the sandbox:

```
services:
  web:
    image: my-stock-room
    ports: ["8080:8080"]          # on all interfaces: it needs a web address
    labels:
      p9m.publish: "true"         # "true" or "1" publishes; anything else does not
      p9m.title: "Stock room"     # optional, at most 80 characters; default: the service name
      p9m.description: "Who took what from the stock room"   # optional, at most 280
```

- A description over several lines keeps its line breaks on the Hub (YAML's `|`):

  ```
  p9m.description: |
    Who took what from the stock room.
    Ask Anna for access.
  ```

- **An image on its card:** `p9m.image: "/screenshot.png"`, a path inside the app (PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, at most 2 MB and 4096 × 4096 pixels). Without it the Hub uses the page's own `<meta property="og:image">` if it has one, and otherwise the title's first letter on a colour. Purgatorium fetches the image in the background straight from the sandbox, only while the app runs (it never wakes an app for it), refreshes it once a day or when the label changes, and never fetches anything from another site: a URL in the label, or an og:image on another host, is ignored.

- What is published is the app's **web address**, the one its sandbox's *Apps* tab shows; with several ports, the lowest one published on all interfaces. A published container with no such port is not on the Hub: the sandbox's *Details* tab warns *published, but has no web address*.

- It appears on the Hub within half a minute, without approval. Remove the label (and deploy again) to take it off; archiving the sandbox does too. Deep sleep keeps it on the Hub.

- Apps started by hand or by an agent count as well: Purgatorium reads the labels from the sandbox's own Docker.

- On the *Apps* tab, a published app has an **On the Hub** marker.

## Votes

Everyone signed in to the Hub can vote for an app once (👍), their own too (as a GitHub star), and take the vote back. The Hub sorts by votes (*Popular*) or by date (*New*); only the count is shown, not who voted. Votes stay when an app leaves the Hub and count on if it is published again at the same address.

## Feed

The Hub has an RSS feed (`/feed.xml`) and a JSON Feed (`/feed.json`), so a new app shows up by itself where the team looks: a Slack, Teams or Mattermost channel (their RSS integrations), Linkwarden, an RSS reader, or n8n and bots for anything else.

Readers cannot sign in, so the feed takes a secret key: the administrator creates the link in Purgatorium's **Overview → Hub feed → Create feed link**. Only the key's hash is kept, so the link is shown once; creating a new one ends the old link. Without the key the feed answers 404.

## Not yet

A webhook on new apps, a Hub per team (with teams), and a Hub open on the internal network without signing in are on the [roadmap](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/roadmap/index.md).

## App access

An app open only to its owner (`p9m.access: owner`, see [App access](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/app-access/index.md)) is not published, even with `p9m.publish`: its **Details** tab says so. A `domain` app shows to Hub viewers who can sign in to Purgatorium itself; viewers allowed only on the Hub (`HUB_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`, `HUB_ALLOWED_EMAILS`) see public apps only. Opening a `domain` app makes the usual sign-in hop.

# App access

By default every web app in a sandbox is public: anyone with its address opens it. A builder can choose, app by app, who opens it, with a label on the app's container:

| `p9m.access` | Who opens the app's web address                                                                                                      |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `public`     | Anyone.                                                                                                                              |
| `domain`     | Anyone who can sign in to this Purgatorium (its sign-in allowlist, `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` and `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS`), and the admin. |
| `owner`      | The sandbox's owner, and the admin.                                                                                                  |

```
services:
  admin:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    labels:
      p9m.access: owner     # or domain, or public
```

An app without the label gets the server's default, `APPS_ACCESS_DEFAULT` (`public` unless set; a company may set `domain`). A value that is not one of the three (a typo such as `privat`) means `owner`, and the sandbox's **Details** tab says so. The **Apps** tab marks each app that is not public: *Owner only*, *Your domain*.

## What a visitor sees

The first time someone opens an app that is not public, their browser makes a short hop to Purgatorium: they sign in if they are not signed in yet, and come straight back to the app. That gives them a cookie for that one app's address, for 8 hours. Someone who may not open it sees a page that says so (*This app is open only to its owner*) and which account they are signed in with.

Purgatorium's own sign-in never reaches an app: the cookie an app's address gets says only that this person may view this app, and Purgatorium takes it off every request before the app sees it, so an app cannot use it to act as its visitor.

An asleep app is woken only for someone who may open it: an anonymous visitor of an owner-only app gets the sign-in hop, not a waking sandbox.

## The app knows who is viewing

Behind `domain` and `owner`, every request to the app carries `X-P9m-User: <their e-mail>` (`admin` for the admin). An app can greet its visitor with it, or use it as its own sign-in. Purgatorium removes an `X-P9m-User` that a visitor sends themselves, also for public apps, so the header can be trusted, but only behind Purgatorium.

## Not covered

- **The TCP addresses** (databases, SSH, Docker) are not HTTP: this does not apply to them. They are protected by their own TLS certificates and passwords, as before; see [Isolation and TCP addresses](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/networking/index.md).
- **Other sandboxes on the internal network.** A port published on all interfaces is also reachable from other sandboxes directly on the internal `traefik-net` address ([Isolation and TCP addresses](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/networking/index.md)), without going through Purgatorium's check. App access protects the web address, not that path: for an app no other sandbox must reach, publish its port on `127.0.0.1` and nothing else (it then has no web address either).
- **Webhooks and API clients without a browser** cannot make the sign-in hop. Keep an app that receives webhooks, or that a script or a mobile app calls, `public` for now.
- **A coding agent's own `curl`** to an app that is not public gets the sign-in redirect. The agent checks whether an app answers from inside (`GET /sandboxes/:name` → `apps[].answers`), which is not affected.

## Timing and failures

- A new or changed label applies within about 12 seconds of the deploy (Purgatorium reads the running sandboxes' labels every 10 s; Traefik asks Purgatorium every 2 s). Until then the sandbox goes by what Purgatorium last knew of it: in a sandbox whose apps were all public, a newly deployed `owner` app is open for those seconds. For an app that must never be open, not even briefly, publish its port on `127.0.0.1` first and on all interfaces only after a few seconds, or deploy it into a sandbox that already has a `domain` or `owner` app.
- A sandbox whose apps are all public does not depend on Purgatorium while it runs, as before. One with a `domain` or `owner` app does: while Purgatorium is down, those apps do not open (it fails closed); public sandboxes keep working.
- The check is per sandbox (one router serves all its apps): in a sandbox with a `domain` or `owner` app, its **public** apps also need Purgatorium. Keep an app that must stay reachable while Purgatorium is down (a webhook receiver, a status page) in a sandbox whose apps are all public.
- If Traefik restarts while Purgatorium is down, no sandbox app opens until Purgatorium is back (Traefik has not yet read the access middlewares).

## On the Hub

An owner-only app is not published on the [Hub](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/hub/index.md), even with `p9m.publish` (the **Details** tab says so: set `p9m.access: domain`). A `domain` app shows to Hub viewers who can sign in to Purgatorium itself; viewers who can sign in only to the Hub (`HUB_ALLOWED_*`) see the public apps.

## Settings

| Variable              | Default   |                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `APPS_ACCESS_DEFAULT` | `public`  | The level of an app without `p9m.access`: `public`, `domain` or `owner`.                                                              |
| `APP_ACCESS_SECRET`   | generated | Signs the app cookies and the one-time sign-in tickets. Without it Purgatorium generates one into `data/app-access.key` and keeps it. |
# Agents

# Let your agent deploy

Give a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…) a personal access token and a sandbox, and it can ship your app there on its own: wake the sandbox, deploy a compose project to the sandbox's own Docker daemon, build images inside it, read the logs and roll out new versions. The app gets its public URL from the tunnel.

1. In the UI: create a sandbox (say `shop`), then in its panel's **Access** tab **Token for this sandbox…** — a token that works only for that sandbox.
1. **Download p9m.env** in the token's dialog and save it in your project folder (keep it out of git), then tell the agent: *Deploy this app to my Purgatorium sandbox — settings in p9m.env.* The file holds `P9M_URL`, `P9M_TOKEN`, `P9M_SANDBOX` and `P9M_AGENT_GUIDE`. Or tell the agent everything yourself, for example:

> Deploy this repo to my Purgatorium sandbox `p9m-shop` at `https://p9m.example.com` with the token `p9m_…`. Follow https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/latest/agent-guide/index.md.

[docs/agent-guide.md](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/agent-guide/index.md) is written for the agent: every call it needs, tried against a live Purgatorium. A token limited to one sandbox keeps the agent away from your other sandboxes; a token for all your sandboxes (Access tokens → + New token) acts as you.

An agent with MCP can also use Purgatorium as an MCP server with the same token: see [MCP](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/mcp/index.md). In Claude Code, the [p9m plugin](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/claude-plugin/index.md) needs no token typed in: install it once (`/plugin marketplace add csakaszamok/p9m`, `/plugin install p9m@p9m`), then run `/p9m:init <address> <sandbox>` in the project and approve in the browser.

## Docker, registry, export

A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex…) can work on a sandbox with plain `docker` commands:

- **Docker from outside:** `<raw>-docker.<domain>:443` reaches the sandbox's own Docker daemon. Purgatorium does not open that TLS: it only reads the name and passes the connection through, so the Docker command line and the sandbox talk to each other with the sandbox's own certificates (only whoever holds its client key gets in). It does not wake a sleeping sandbox (wake it first: **Wake**, `POST /sandboxes/:name/start`, or the MCP tool `wake_sandbox`); traffic on the connection keeps a running one awake, a connection that is only open (e.g. Docker Desktop keeping a context connected) does not.
- **Let your agent deploy…**, on a sandbox's **Apps** tab (and in the Advanced view also at the top of its **Access** tab), is the same window in both views. For the [Claude Code plugin](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/claude-plugin/index.md): the two lines that install it (once), and the `/p9m:init <address> <sandbox>` line to paste into Claude Code in the project; you approve in the browser, and the project gets its `.p9m` folder with a token for the sandbox. For other agents: **Download** gives `p9m-<raw>.zip`, with a `.p9m` folder to unpack in the project's root folder (its own `.gitignore` of `*` keeps it out of git; add `.p9m` to `.dockerignore` too, so that a build never copies it into an image), and what to tell the agent (*set up the p9m zip from my Downloads in this project and deploy*). Before a sandbox has Docker access it offers to enable it, or to export without the Docker keys. In the Advanced view the window has **Options**: the token's name and expiry (for the zip), a zip without the Docker keys, and **Copy as .env**, which puts `p9m.env` (a new token for the sandbox) on the clipboard. When the sandbox's Portainer is public, both also carry `P9M_PORTAINER_URL` and a Portainer API token (`P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN`, sent as `X-API-Key`), made for the export, so the agent never gets the Portainer admin password; making it wakes the sandbox. That token does not expire and revoking the Purgatorium token does not revoke it: delete it in the sandbox's Portainer (My account → Access tokens). The `.p9m` folder holds `p9m.env` (with a new token limited to the sandbox, `P9M_DOCKER_HOST`, `P9M_REGISTRY`), the Docker client keys and a README with the `docker context create` command for Windows and macOS/Linux. It is a secret; **Rotate Docker keys…** makes the keys of earlier exports useless.
- **Registry:** `docker login registry.<domain>` with a Purgatorium token as the password (a token limited to a sandbox pushes to `<raw>/…`, a personal one to its owner's sandboxes); the password returned at create still works.
- **Anonymous pull after a secret scan:** every push is scanned (files such as `.env`, private keys, and well-known key formats, in every layer and in the image config, where Dockerfile `ENV` lines end up). Anonymous pull is decided per repository: one whose versions are all clean — and that has nothing in the registry Purgatorium has not scanned — can be pulled by anyone without logging in; one flagged, unscanned or failed version keeps the whole repository private until it is deleted. The registry tells Purgatorium about pushes with a secret Purgatorium generates (`data/registry-notify.secret`). Garbage collection runs weekly; a push at that very moment may fail and needs a retry. The **Registry** tab shows the images, the scan results (masked) and a Delete button. `REGISTRY_PUBLIC_PULL=false` keeps everything private.

## An agent inside a sandbox

A coding agent can also run inside one sandbox (say, in a VS Code or code-server container there) and deploy to another: give it that other sandbox's access as usual (the [Claude Code plugin](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/claude-plugin/index.md) with `/p9m:init` for that sandbox, or its zip). It needs two names to reach from inside the sandbox: Purgatorium's (`p9m.<domain>`, the API and MCP) and the other sandbox's Docker address (`<sandbox>-docker.<domain>`), plus its apps' addresses if it opens them.

**With a real domain** (a wildcard DNS record for `*.<domain>`), these names point at the server from inside a sandbox too: nothing to set. The server must reach its own public address from inside, which it usually does ("hairpin NAT"; most clouds and Docker do it).

**On a local development stack on `lvh.me`** they do not: `lvh.me` names point at `127.0.0.1`, which inside a sandbox's container is that container itself, not Purgatorium. With Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS), point them at the host, `192.168.65.254` (what `host.docker.internal` resolves to; a fixed address), with `extra_hosts` on the agent's service in that sandbox's compose file:

```
    extra_hosts:
      - "p9m.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"
      - "shop-docker.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"   # the other sandbox's Docker address
      - "shop-web.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"      # its app, if the agent opens it
```

It has to be an address: `extra_hosts` takes no names, and `host-gateway` inside a sandbox is the sandbox's own container, not the host. The names stay as they are, because the TLS certificates and Traefik's routing go by them. On a Linux host without Docker Desktop there is no such address: use a real domain there.

# MCP

[![](../media/mcp-agent-poster.webp)](../media/mcp-agent.mp4)

The same API is an MCP server at `/mcp` (Streamable HTTP): each endpoint is a tool, such as `list_sandboxes`, `create_sandbox`, `wake_sandbox`, `sleep_sandbox`, `get_sandbox` (with its app links), `set_sleep_settings`, and for the sandbox's files `list_sandbox_files`, `read_sandbox_file`, `write_sandbox_file`, `create_sandbox_folder`, `delete_sandbox_file` and `list_sandbox_volumes` (the apps' volumes, whose paths the other file tools take). A tool call runs the endpoint with the caller's token, so it can do exactly what that token can do on the REST API; a token limited to one sandbox stays limited to it, and is offered only the tools it may call (no `create_sandbox`, no token or SSH key management). Only tokens are accepted (not a browser session).

For Claude Code, add it by hand (the [p9m plugin](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/claude-plugin/index.md) is a deploy skill and does not add it):

```
claude mcp add --transport http p9m https://p9m.example.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer p9m_…"
```

Other clients take the same URL and header, e.g. `{"mcpServers": {"p9m": {"type": "http", "url": "https://p9m.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer p9m_…"}}}}`. Left out: the log stream (it never ends) and the zip export (a file a tool result cannot carry).

A client that can only start a local process (stdio) can use `scripts/mcp-stdio.mjs` from this repository: it needs only Node.js 18+, no packages, and passes each message to the server's `/mcp` with your token:

```
{"mcpServers": {"p9m": {"command": "node", "args": ["/path/to/p9m/scripts/mcp-stdio.mjs"], "env": {"P9M_URL": "https://p9m.example.com", "P9M_TOKEN": "p9m_…"}}}}
```

Under the hood it is JSON-RPC over HTTP: one `POST /mcp` per call, no session to open first, so even `curl` can call a tool (`tools/list`, then `tools/call` with the tool's `name` and `arguments`):

[![](../media/mcp-rpc-poster.webp)](../media/mcp-rpc.mp4)

# Claude Code plugin

New to this?

[Put your app online with Claude Code](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/tutorials/claude-code/index.md) walks through it step by step.

The `p9m` plugin teaches Claude Code to deploy: you say *put my app online*, it deploys the project to your sandbox's own Docker, checks that the app answers and gives you its address. The plugin itself keeps no address and no token: each project says which Purgatorium and which sandbox it belongs to, in its own `.p9m` folder.

## Install

Once on your computer, from a terminal (a sandbox's **Let your agent deploy…** shows these lines ready to copy). Claude Code in an editor (the VS Code extension) has no `/plugin`, so there this is the way:

```
claude plugin marketplace add csakaszamok/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m
```

Or in Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add csakaszamok/p9m
/plugin install p9m@p9m
```

Claude Code asks where to install it: **user** (every folder of yours; usually what you want), **project** (this repository, for everyone who uses it, through its `.claude/settings.json`) or **local** (this folder, only you). It asks for nothing else: no address, no token. Updates come with Purgatorium's releases (`/plugin marketplace update p9m`).

## Connect a project: `/p9m:init`

In Claude Code, in the project's root folder, run the line that **Let your agent deploy…** shows for the sandbox:

```
/p9m:init https://p9m.example.com shop
```

Claude Code prints a link. Open it in your browser (sign in first if Purgatorium asks). The page shows a code and the sandbox; check that the code is the one Claude Code printed and click **Approve** (or **Deny**). Only the sandbox's owner (or the admin) can approve. The code works once and expires in 10 minutes.

Then Claude Code unpacks the project's `.p9m` folder straight to disk: a new token for that sandbox only (in `.p9m/p9m.env`, 90 days) and the sandbox's Docker keys. The token never shows on the screen or in the chat. The folder keeps itself out of git, and the token is listed in Purgatorium under **My area → Access tokens** as `Claude Code init <date>`, where you can revoke it.

Run `/p9m:init` again whenever the token has expired or was revoked. A project can be tied to one sandbox at a time; another project in another folder can be tied to another sandbox, or to another Purgatorium.

## The `.p9m` folder

The `.p9m` folder in the project's root folder says which Purgatorium and which sandbox the project belongs to: `p9m.env` (the address, the sandbox's name and its token) and the sandbox's Docker keys. `/p9m:init` writes it, or you unpack it from an export zip. It holds secrets, and it keeps itself out of git: its own `.gitignore` is a single `*`. Add `.p9m` to `.dockerignore` too, so that a build never copies it into an image; the agent does when it writes one.

## Use

In your project's folder, ask in your own words, e.g. *deploy this app to my sandbox* or *give me a link to show this to someone*, or run `/p9m:deploy`. You need Docker installed on your machine (the build runs in the sandbox, but the `docker` command line talks to it). In a project without a `.p9m` folder, the agent tells you to run `/p9m:init` first.

The plugin has two skills:

- **`/p9m:init`**: ties the project to a sandbox, as above;
- **`/p9m:deploy`**: the steps of the [agent guide](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/agent-guide/index.md) in short, for an agent that may be talking to someone who is not a developer. It works from `.p9m/p9m.env` with the REST API, and gets fresh Docker keys through a single-use link (unpacked to the disk, so a key never passes through the model: copied by a model a key gets garbled, and it would end up in the transcript).

The plugin does not bring the MCP server. Purgatorium still has one, for other MCP clients: see [MCP](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/mcp/index.md).

## Where it works

The plugin works fully in Claude Code: in the terminal, and in the Claude desktop app's **Code** tab; also in Claude Code inside a sandbox, deploying to another one (on a local `lvh.me` stack see [An agent inside a sandbox](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/agents/#an-agent-inside-a-sandbox)). Claude chat and Cowork can install it too (**Customize → Plugins**, add the marketplace `csakaszamok/p9m`), but they cannot run commands on your computer, so there it does not do much. Without the plugin, any agent can deploy with an export (**Let your agent deploy…** on a sandbox) or a token: see [Let your agent deploy](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/agents/index.md).

# Purgatorium for agents: deploy and update apps in a sandbox

This guide is for a coding agent (for example Claude Code on the user's machine) that deploys or updates apps in the user's Purgatorium sandbox. Every call below was run against a live Purgatorium.

Every sandbox has its own Docker daemon. The agent works with:

- the **Purgatorium API**, with the user's personal access token, to find the sandbox, wake it and get its Docker client certificates;
- the sandbox's **Docker daemon**, with the plain `docker` command line, to deploy, build and update.

An agent with MCP can make the Purgatorium API calls as tools instead: see [MCP](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/mcp/index.md). A sandbox made from the `portainer` template also has a Portainer API: see [With Portainer](#with-portainer) at the end.

## What the user gives the agent

| Value                 | Example                   | Where it comes from                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Purgatorium URL       | `https://p9m.example.com` | The address of the Purgatorium UI                      |
| Personal access token | `p9m_…`                   | UI → **My area** → **Access tokens** → **+ New token** |
| Sandbox name          | `p9m-shop`                | The name in the UI list with the `p9m-` prefix         |

The user may instead give these in a `p9m.env` file in the project (UI → the new token → **Download p9m.env**; it may also be renamed `.env` or copied into one): `P9M_URL`, `P9M_TOKEN`, `P9M_SANDBOX` (only for a token limited to one sandbox; otherwise ask which sandbox, or list them with `GET /sandboxes`) and `P9M_AGENT_GUIDE` (this guide). Read them from there; do not print the token or commit the file.

The token may be limited to one sandbox. Then `GET /sandboxes` lists only that one, `GET /me` returns it as `sandbox`, and creating or deleting sandboxes answers 403. Everything in this guide works with such a token.

Every Purgatorium API call sends `Authorization: Bearer p9m_…`. The token acts as the user: it sees and changes only the user's own sandboxes.

## 1. Find the sandbox and wake it

```
GET /sandboxes/p9m-shop
```

The answer includes:

- `status`: `running`, `exited` (asleep) or `deep_sleep`;
- `docker_access`: `host`, the address of the sandbox's Docker daemon (for example `shop-docker.example.com`), and `state`: `ready`, or `needs-certs` when its certificates do not cover that address (the user enables it once: **Access → Enable**, which restarts the sandbox); and, while the sandbox is not running, `hint`: a Docker connection does not wake it, so start it first (`docker` would only get EOF);
- with `?include_keys=true` only: `ca_cert`, `client_cert`, `client_key`, the Docker client certificates and private key (PEM). Write them to files with a program (below), never by copying them through a model: copied by hand a key gets garbled (and still looks like a key), and in an answer it goes into the model's context and transcript. A single-use link (below) puts them on disk without them passing through an answer;
- `tunnel_urls`: the app addresses.

If `status` is not `running`, wake the sandbox and poll until it is:

```
POST /sandboxes/p9m-shop/start
GET  /sandboxes/p9m-shop        → repeat until "status": "running"
```

Waking from `exited` takes a few seconds; from `deep_sleep` about 30 seconds. Connecting to the Docker daemon does **not** wake it: while the sandbox sleeps, `docker` fails to connect (connection reset or EOF), so wake it first.

A request to an app address while the sandbox is not ready returns an HTML **waiting page** ("Sandbox is waking up") with status 200, instead of the real answer: treat it as "not ready yet" and retry after a few seconds.

## 2. Connect the docker command line

Ask for a single-use link to the project's `.p9m` folder (MCP: `project_dir_link`). Purgatorium checks the keys first; the link works once, for 5 minutes:

```
POST /sandboxes/p9m-shop/project-link
→ { "url": "https://p9m.example.com/project-dir/…", "expires_in": 300,
    "command": "curl -sf \"https://p9m.example.com/project-dir/…\" | tar -x -C <project folder>",
    "context_commands": ["docker context rm -f p9m-shop", "docker context create p9m-shop --docker \"host=tcp://shop-docker.example.com:443,ca=<project folder>/.p9m/docker/ca.pem,…\""] }
```

Run `command`, then `context_commands`, with the project's root folder for `<project folder>`. The download writes `.p9m/.gitignore` (`*`: git leaves the folder out), `.p9m/p9m.env` (`P9M_URL`, `P9M_SANDBOX`, `P9M_DOCKER_HOST`) and `.p9m/docker/{ca,cert,key}.pem`. On Windows: `curl.exe --ssl-no-revoke`; `tar` comes with Windows 10 and later. A used or expired link answers **410**: ask for a new one.

```
docker --context p9m-shop compose ls
```

A context keeps its own copies of the files: after new keys run both again, with a new link. Check it with a compose command, as above: `ps` can work with a key that compose cannot read (`tls: failed to parse private key`). On a TLS error get a new link; do not repair a key file. Add `.p9m` to `.dockerignore`, so that a build never copies the keys into an image.

Only TLS with these certificates gets in: Purgatorium passes the connection through without opening it. Keep the key as secret as the token.

If the user gave you an export instead, it is a `.p9m` folder for the project's root folder (from the zip `p9m-<sandbox>.zip`; an older export is a `p9m-<sandbox>/` folder): `p9m.env`, `docker/` with the certificates, a README, and a `.gitignore` of `*` that keeps the folder out of git. `p9m.env` has `P9M_DOCKER_HOST`. Unpack a zip into the project's root and delete the zip (it holds a token); add `.p9m` to `.dockerignore`, so that a build never copies the keys into an image:

```
docker context create p9m-shop --docker "host=$P9M_DOCKER_HOST,ca=$PWD/.p9m/docker/ca.pem,cert=$PWD/.p9m/docker/cert.pem,key=$PWD/.p9m/docker/key.pem"
```

## 3. Deploy an app

A compose project in the sandbox, built and run there:

```
docker --context p9m-shop compose -p shop up -d --build
```

```
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    labels:
      p9m.subdomain: shop
```

- **Publish ports on all interfaces** (`8080:8080`): that is what gives the app its public address. A port published on `127.0.0.1` stays private to the sandbox: no address at all. The app itself must listen on `0.0.0.0` inside its container (not `127.0.0.1`), or its address answers with an error; `GET /sandboxes/:name` → `apps[].answers` says whether it answers. An app labelled `p9m.access: domain` or `owner` ([App access](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/app-access/index.md)) answers your own `curl` with a redirect to Purgatorium's sign-in: check `apps[].answers` instead. Set the label the user asks for (*only for me* → `owner`, *for my colleagues* → `domain`) before the first deploy.
- **Set a restart policy** (`restart: unless-stopped`): when the sandbox wakes from sleep, only containers with one start again.
- Pass secrets when the container runs (`environment:`, `env_file:` read on your machine by `docker compose`), **never in the image**.

### The app's public address

Every published TCP port gets an HTTP address. With the sandbox `p9m-shop` on `example.com`:

- with a `p9m.subdomain: shop` label: `https://shop-shop.example.com`, that is `<sandbox>-<subdomain>.<domain>`;
- without the label: `https://shop-<project>-<container>-port<host port>.example.com`. The container name is `<project>-<service>-1` unless `container_name` is set.

The app is reachable a few seconds after the container starts. `GET /sandboxes/p9m-shop` lists the addresses in `tunnel_urls`.

A database or other TCP service published the same way also gets a TLS address on port 443: see [Isolation and TCP addresses](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/networking/#tls-tcp-addresses).

## 4. Update the app

Change the code or the image tag and run the same `docker --context p9m-shop compose -p shop up -d --build` again: compose recreates the changed containers and keeps the volumes. Use a fixed tag for every release (`:1.4.2`, `:1.4.3`, …) so you can roll back by deploying the previous one.

### Push to the registry

Every sandbox can push to Purgatorium's registry, so an image can be pulled elsewhere too:

```
docker login registry.example.com -u shop             # password: the token
docker --context p9m-shop tag shop-web registry.example.com/shop/web:3
docker --context p9m-shop push registry.example.com/shop/web:3
```

- Every push is scanned for secrets, and an image with a `.env` file or a key in it stays private (`GET /sandboxes/<name>/registry` shows what was found).
- Anyone can pull the image from any machine (`docker pull registry.<domain>/shop/web:3`) once **every** version of it passed the scan: one flagged version keeps the whole image private until it is deleted.

## 5. Other ways in

- **SSH:** `ssh root@<sandbox>-shell-tcp.<domain>` through port 443 ([SSH, terminal and logs](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/shell-and-logs/index.md)); inside, `docker` talks to the sandbox's Docker.
- **Logs** of every app in the sandbox: `GET /sandboxes/<name>/logs/stream` (Server-Sent Events).

## With Portainer

A sandbox made from the `portainer` template (or one with Portainer in its own compose) also has Portainer, which proxies the sandbox's Docker daemon over HTTPS: an agent can deploy through its API without the `docker` command line. `GET /sandboxes/<name>` then has:

- `extras.portainer_url`, for example `https://shop-portainer.example.com` (if its host is not in `tunnel_urls`, Portainer is published on `127.0.0.1` and private to the sandbox: ask the user to publish it on all interfaces, `9000:9000`, in **Starter stack…**);
- `extras.portainer_password` (user `admin`).

`GET <portainer_url>/api/status` returning JSON means Portainer is ready (an HTML answer is the waiting page). Portainer traffic wakes an asleep sandbox and keeps it awake.

### Sign in to Portainer

If `p9m.env` has `P9M_PORTAINER_URL` and `P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN`, skip the sign-in: use `P9M_PORTAINER_URL` as `<portainer_url>` and send `X-API-Key: <P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN>` instead of `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on every Portainer call below. (A line `# Portainer: not included (…)` says why there is none; then sign in as below, or use the Docker command line, [2](#2-connect-the-docker-command-line).)

Otherwise sign in with `extras.portainer_password`:

```
POST <portainer_url>/api/auth
Content-Type: application/json

{"username": "admin", "password": "<extras.portainer_password>"}
```

The answer is `{"jwt": "…"}`. Send `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on every Portainer call below.

Then find the environment (endpoint) ID. It is the sandbox's Docker daemon, usually `1`:

```
GET <portainer_url>/api/endpoints      → [{"Id": 1, "Name": "primary", …}]
```

If the list is empty (nobody clicked **Get started** in the Portainer UI yet), create the environment once:

```
POST <portainer_url>/api/endpoints
Content-Type: multipart/form-data

Name=local
EndpointCreationType=1
```

### Deploy an app as a stack

A Portainer stack is a compose project that Portainer can update later. Deploy it from compose text:

```
POST <portainer_url>/api/stacks/create/standalone/string?endpointId=1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "shop",
  "stackFileContent": "services:\n  web:\n    image: registry.example.com/shop:1.4.2\n    ports: [\"8080:8080\"]\n    labels:\n      p9m.subdomain: shop\n",
  "env": [{"name": "LOG_LEVEL", "value": "info"}]
}
```

The answer includes the stack `Id`; keep it for updates. `GET <portainer_url>/api/stacks` lists the stacks with their IDs.

The same rules hold as in [3. Deploy an app](#3-deploy-an-app): publish ports on all interfaces, set a restart policy.

### Update a stack

Change the image tag in the compose text and redeploy. `pullImage: true` pulls the image again even if the tag did not change (for `:latest`):

```
PUT <portainer_url>/api/stacks/<stack id>?endpointId=1
Content-Type: application/json

{"stackFileContent": "<the full compose text>", "env": [], "prune": true, "pullImage": true}
```

`prune: true` removes services that are no longer in the compose text. Portainer recreates the changed containers; the volumes are kept.

To build in the sandbox, send the build context as a tar archive to the Docker build endpoint through Portainer's Docker proxy:

```
POST <portainer_url>/api/endpoints/1/docker/build?t=shop:1.4.3
Content-Type: application/x-tar

<tar of the directory with the Dockerfile>
```

The answer streams the build log as JSON lines; the last line is `{"stream":"Successfully tagged shop:1.4.3\n"}` on success, or an `{"error": …}` line on failure. Then redeploy the stack with `image: shop:1.4.3` and `pullImage: false` (the image only exists locally).

### Everything else Docker can do

`<portainer_url>/api/endpoints/1/docker/<Docker Engine API path>` is the sandbox's Docker Engine API. Examples:

| Call                                                             | Docker Engine API       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `GET …/docker/containers/json`                                   | list running containers |
| `GET …/docker/containers/<name>/logs?stdout=1&stderr=1&tail=200` | container logs          |
| `POST …/docker/containers/<name>/restart`                        | restart a container     |
| `POST …/docker/images/create?fromImage=alpine&tag=3.20`          | pull an image           |
| `DELETE …/docker/images/<image>`                                 | remove an image         |

The stack Purgatorium deployed when it created the sandbox (Portainer + `http-echo`) was deployed with `docker compose` outside Portainer: Portainer shows it but cannot edit it as a stack.

## Things to keep in mind

- **Sleep:** the sandbox sleeps after its idle timeout without HTTP traffic, 30 minutes by default. The user can change this or turn it off in the UI (**Sleep settings…**) or with `PATCH /sandboxes/<name>` `{"idle_timeout": "2h"}`, where `0` or `off` means never. Docker traffic keeps a running sandbox awake (a build, `docker logs -f`, a pull), but a connection that is only open does not; plain HTTP traffic to its apps (or to Portainer) counts too.
- **Archive** (`DELETE /sandboxes/<name>`, **Archive…** in the UI) archives the sandbox: its configuration and data are kept in the archive, and it is removed from the list.
- **The Purgatorium API reference** is at `<Purgatorium URL>/swagger`.
# Reference

# API

[![](../media/api-curl-poster.webp)](../media/api-curl.mp4)

| Method   | Path                                       | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes`                               | Create a sandbox (`name`; optional `runtime` like `dind`, `template` like `starter`, `compose` (your own compose text instead of the template's; its `before_script` and defaults still apply), `idle_timeout` like `30m`, `deep_sleep_after` like `7d` or `off`, `ssh_keys` (extra SSH public keys for this sandbox only), `cpus` like `2`, `memory` like `4g`, `create_inner_stack: false` for no template stack)                        |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes`                               | List all sandboxes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/summary`                       | How many sandboxes: `quota`, `total`, `free`, `running`, `asleep`, `deep_sleep`, `archived`; your own (and `server_full`), or for the admin the whole server, `by_owner`, `server_limit` / `server_used` and `resources` (not with a token limited to one sandbox)                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name`                         | Get sandbox details; the Docker client certificates and key (`ca_cert`, `client_cert`, `client_key`) only with `?include_keys=true`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/compose`                 | The starter stack deployed into the sandbox (compose YAML), secrets masked (**Starter stack…** in the UI)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `PATCH`  | `/sandboxes/:name`                         | Change `idle_timeout` and/or `deep_sleep_after` (see [Sleep and wake](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/sleep-wake/index.md)), `cpus` and/or `memory` (see [CPU and memory](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/resources/#cpu-and-memory))                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/start`                   | Wake a sandbox, also from deep sleep (**Wake** in the UI); 409 at the owner's limit with `reason` and `running`; `{"sleep": "<name>"}` puts that running one to sleep first                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/stop`                    | Put a sandbox to sleep now (**Sleep** in the UI)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/deep-sleep`              | Put a sandbox into deep sleep now, also a running one (**Deep sleep now** on the panel's **Details** tab)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/keep-awake`              | Start a running sandbox's sleep countdown over (**Reset** next to *Sleeps in*); 409 if it is not running                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/export`                  | A zip for coding agents: a new token for the sandbox, its Docker client keys, a README (owner/admin; not with a token limited to one sandbox); `docker: false` without the keys, `format: "env"` the p9m.env text                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/project-link`            | A single-use link (5 minutes) to the project's `.p9m` folder with the Docker client keys, checked first; answers `url`, `command` (`curl … \| tar -x`) and `context_commands`, never the keys                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `GET`    | `/project-dir/:token`                      | The `.p9m` folder as a tar, once (no token: the link is the authorization); `410` when used or expired                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `POST`   | `/device/code`                             | Start a device approval for `/p9m:init` (no token; `sandbox` optional): answers `device_code` (the agent's secret), `user_code`, `verification_uri_complete`, `expires_in` (600) and `interval` (3); both codes live 10 minutes                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `POST`   | `/device/poll`                             | Ask whether it was approved (no token; `device_code` in the body): `{"status": "pending"}` or `"denied"`, `410` `"expired"` (also for a used code), or `approved` with the same answer as `project-link`, once                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `GET`    | `/activate`                                | The page where a signed-in owner approves or denies a code (`?code=`); `POST` sends the decision                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/docker-keys`             | New Docker access certificates (**Enable** / **Rotate Docker keys…**); restarts the sandbox                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/registry`                | The sandbox's images in the registry, with secret-scan results                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `DELETE` | `/sandboxes/:name/registry/:app/:digest`   | Delete one version of an image                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/restart`                 | Restart a sandbox                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files`                   | List a folder of the sandbox's files (`path`, default `/root`): `/root`, `/home`, `/srv` and `/opt`, the folders kept over a deep sleep, and the apps' volumes; the sandbox must be running (409 `not_running` otherwise). See [Files](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/files/index.md)                                                                                                                                              |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/content`           | Download a file (`path`), or a folder as a tar                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `PUT`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/content`           | Upload a file to `path` (the body is the file; missing folders on the path are made), up to `FILES_MAX_UPLOAD`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/files/text`              | A text file's content as JSON (UTF-8, up to 1 MB): for agents                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/files/mkdir`             | Create a folder (`{"path": "/srv/data"}`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `DELETE` | `/sandboxes/:name/files`                   | Delete a file or a folder (`path`), not the four folders themselves (nor a volume's folder)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/volumes`                 | The volumes of the apps in the sandbox's own Docker: `name`, `path` (for the routes above), `project`, `containers` that use it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `GET`    | `/sandboxes/:name/mounts`                  | The host folders mounted into the sandbox: `mounts` (`host`, `target`, `readonly`), `enabled` (`HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS` is set); the admin also gets `roots`. Owner, admin, and a token limited to the sandbox. See [Host folders](https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/0.12/web-ui/#host-folders)                                                                                                                                                  |
| `POST`   | `/sandboxes/:name/mounts`                  | Mount a host folder (admin only, `HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS` set, else 403 / 409): `{"host": "/srv/shared/team", "target": "/mnt/team", "readonly": true}`, `target` defaulting to `/mnt/<last part of host>`.
